Patina · the client approval experience

The Decision,
Walked

The homeowner's approval, from the letter to the record — the same seven steps in her inbox, on her page, and in her hand.

What changed: an approval from her studio stopped being a notice she clears and became a letter she answers — one question, three acts of equal weight, a name typed and held, and a stamp she can keep.

Words

The words she reads, and the words she never reads

She reads

Approval is the ask. Decision is only a choice between named alternatives, or the record as a whole. Five words settle a thing, and each is drawn as a mark:

Approved Returned Held Chosen Signed

In prose they lower-case: she approved, she returned, she held. Never “Declined” for a return.

She never reads

Gate. Task. Overdue. Dashboard. No guilt, no apology, no invented timing, and no numbers where words will do — eight approvals wait on her, not 8.

A date that has passed says Due September 1 · past its date in body ink, never red. The letter that follows says Still open, Leah asked on August 24.

Terracotta survives exactly once in the whole system, as Declined, with no green counterpart anywhere.

The letter · one of three

The first notice reads like one

Leah sent “Kitchen plan set” for your approval “The island moved a foot; everything else is as we drew it.” — Leah Edition 3 · issued September 1 Due Saturday, September 12. — Leah, Middle West Studio

The studio signs the mail: designer's given name, studio name, and the city on the line beneath — omitted when it isn't known. With neither a person nor a studio to name, the letter goes unsigned rather than signed “Patina”.

One announcement, once. The forty-eight-hour cron always speaks in the reminder register, so an approval already in flight never hears “sent” late.

The designer's one-line why is frozen with the edition and attributed to whoever wrote it. No checksum in the body — an edition and a date instead.

Where the link lands

client.patina.cloud/decisions/{id}

On a phone with Patina installed, that address opens the approval itself. In a browser it lands on the anchor for that approval on her own page, after sign-in — the link survives the sign-in and takes her back. There is no login-less door.

The letter · two of three

The reminder, and the notice that follows it

Saturday: “Kitchen plan set” “Kitchen plan set” is still open and due Saturday. Nothing has changed since it was sent.
Still open: “Kitchen plan set” Still open, Leah asked on September 2.

With no name to use: Still open, your designer asked on September 2.

The reminder names the weekday, because that is how she holds a date. Its last sentence is dropped the moment a new edition has been issued — something has changed, and the letter will not say otherwise.

Nothing is called overdue. Nothing warns. And after that notice Patina goes quiet: no third letter, no escalation, no count of days.

The hours

Approval mail waits for the morning — nothing before 8am in her time zone. Her phone keeps the same hours and stops at 8pm. The notice that an approval has passed its date is the one thing that never waits.

The letter · three of three

The receipt names the real consequence, or says nothing

You approved “Kitchen plan set”. It releases Walnut dining table, 96″. The record: client.patina.cloud/decisions/… — Leah, Middle West Studio
You returned “Kitchen plan set”. Your answer is on the record.

Three pieces waiting on one approval read as “It releases three pieces that were waiting on it.” Where no honest consequence exists, the sentence is simply absent. Nothing is invented to make the act feel bigger.

There is no button on a receipt — a plain link to the record, and no request that she come back and look at anything.

Its push is silent

The acknowledgment of her own act carries no sound and moves no number. She already knows what she did.

A return is returned in prose, everywhere. Never declined.

The client page · 01

She signs in and stands at the doorstep

There is no home screen and no list of things to clear. Her page is the project, written down the left as a story pole — Design, Design refinement, Installation, Completion — with a mark where the house actually stands.

One sentence at the top says what is waiting on her. Beneath it the money stands plainly, then the letterbox, then her approval. Nothing is counted at her and nothing is called a dashboard.

The same page at desk width puts the story pole beside the reading column rather than above it.

The client page · 02

The plate, the why, and the weighing

The artifact is a plate, named and dated: Edition 901 · Issued September 5. The question is the heading, and it belongs to a person — the designer's one-line why sits under it, signed.

Then the weighing. One sentence first: the cost rises by $1,250, the schedule moves out by three days, and the lead time grows by seven days. The three deltas stand beside it as figures, independently, so a zero is stated rather than hidden. No color encodes direction.

Three acts follow, the same size, each saying what it does before she touches it.

The client page · 03

Return asks for a note, and says where it goes

Choosing Return names the consequence first: send this edition back for revision and a new approval request. Then it asks for the note, and tells her where the note lands rather than scolding her for its absence.

The submit simply stays unlit until she writes something. No red, no asterisk, no word “required”.

No name is asked. A signature to say “this needs discussion” would be theatre; a press-and-hold is enough. Hold behaves the same way, with no note and no name — nothing moves, and the studio comes to her.

Her note appears immediately under The Discussion, dated, in her own second person.

The client page · 04

Approve: your name, and then the hold

Only Approve raises the signature line. Her full legal name goes on a rule with the date at its right end, and one sentence makes the typing count.

Then the press. A tap sends nothing. The hold fills over about nine tenths of a second; let go early and it empties and nothing is recorded. A keyboard holds too — Enter, held, does the same thing.

Under reduced motion the ink arrives at once and leaves at once. A motion preference never costs her a longer gesture.

Her name is written down with the act: an approval records an electronic signature; a return or a hold records a press-through, and never nothing at all.

The client page · 05

The stamp settles, and the line resumes

The doors go and a mark takes their place. It is drawn the way paper is stamped: a mono word, a hairline rule, no fill, a little over a degree off square, in mocha ink.

The eyebrow above it changes from YOUR ANSWER IS NEEDED to ANSWERED, and the standing sentence at the top of her page recomposes without the clause that named this paper. That is the reward, and it is the honest one.

The settle plays once, in the session where she answered. On every later visit the stamp is simply there. A stamp that re-animates on each load is a badge pretending to be paper.

The client page · 06

A paper that needs her name is a door

The act is held on two things at once: the consent tick and the typed name. A plain click yields nothing. A held press swings the door — about half a second — and the head reopens: Open. It opened on your name.

The receipt beneath names the studio, never the nearest person:

Aspen Loft — Addendum No. 1 · signed 6 September · Leah Hartwell has your signature. You’ll have a copy.

Further down, an approval past its date reads “This one is past its date, so its notice stands.” Its Remind-me block is gone, and the server refuses a snooze there too.

The client page · 07

Previously, and the Record of Decision

Answered work does not disappear. It folds into Previously, where each settled edition keeps its mark, and where a superseded edition carries one act — forward, to the edition that replaced it, never backward.

Keep a copy builds the sheet above. It says how she answered, and only what it can source: Signed electronically by typed name for an approval she signed, Confirmed by press-and-hold for one she returned, and simply Recorded where the row cannot say more.

Printing drops the cream, stands the stamp upright, and takes the shadows out. No IP address appears anywhere on it. A stranger asking for the same address is told the record could not be found — the same sentence the owner gets for an id that names nothing.

The client page · 08

She sets the pace

Three cadences, hers to choose: tell me right away, once a day, once a week on Sunday. Beside them the floor is stated in plain words, including the two things that ignore it — the weekly summary, and the notice that an approval has passed its date.

On an open approval, Remind me holds the reminders without touching the answer: tomorrow morning, Sunday, when it’s due, or don’t remind me. The said-line is honest about its carve-outs: if the date passes or a new edition arrives, I’ll still say so.

Chosen after midnight, “tomorrow morning” means the next 8am — hours away, not the calendar day after.

The app · 01

Today, and the row that needs her

The app opens on Today. NEEDS YOU carries what is owed — an open obligation does not age out of view. Each row says who asked and by when, in words.

MOVED carries what happened, including what she did: You approved the plan set. Her own act, in second person, dated honestly, with the mark it earned. It ages out on the same seven-day window as everything else — no tombstone, no special case.

The tab bar carries no badge. The only number Patina moves is on the home-screen icon.

The app · 02

The approval in her hand

The same ceremony, one type step down. The eyebrow says APPROVAL, never decision — a decision is a choice between named things, and this is an ask.

The question is the heading. The why sits beneath it, signed. Then the edition and its date, the sentence that fixes exactly what she is answering, and the deltas stated one under another.

Three acts, full width, equal weight, in the order they always appear. Choose one outcome. Below them, a way to talk to her designer that submits nothing.

The app · 03

Return on the phone

The composer is already open, and the ask is softer than the web’s: Optional. Your note goes with this returned edition.

The asymmetry is deliberate. On a desk, a change request without a note is a dead end for the studio, so the page requires one. On a phone, holding a thumb at a keyboard to say “not yet” is a toll, so the app encourages instead.

Her designer is named once, in the field itself. Nothing repeats the name in the line beneath it.

Hold behaves the same way with no note at all — the studio reaches out, and nothing moves in the meantime.

The app · 04

The name, the hold, the stamp

Choosing Approve raises the signature rule and only then: her name, the date at the right, and the sentence that makes the typing count. Return and Hold never see it.

One press of about a second and a half records the answer. A tap does not. Beneath the act, Choose another outcome stays available until she commits — nothing about the ceremony traps her.

Then the doors are gone, the mark is there, and one sentence tells her what she did in her own second person.

The mark never fills, never gains a checkmark, and never turns green.

The app · 05

The sign act, and the seal at the end of it

A proposal signs full screen. The studio’s own terms print verbatim, in the studio’s own sentence case — Patina does not retype them.

When the act completes, a cover arrives and the seal settles into it: the mark, her name beneath in mono, and one sentence. Nobody countersigns anything; the studio holds her signature and she will have a copy.

Under reduced motion the cover arrives in a single frame and the mark cross-fades in place — no slide, no travel.

If a signature cannot be recorded, the refusal is body ink, not red: We couldn’t record your signature. Nothing has been signed.

The app · 06

Keep a copy

Every settled thing keeps a paper, and the act to get it sits right under the mark. It builds the same Record of Decision the web prints and hands it straight to the share sheet, ready to save or send.

The sheet carries the studio’s letterhead, the edition, the question, the mark upright, and how she answered. A twelve-character reference sits at the foot of an approval’s record; a proposal has no edition to reference, so it prints none rather than inventing one.

It reads the same on both surfaces. The keepsake is not a second design.

The app · 07

When the studio offers a choice

Two options sit abreast at exactly the same size. Three or more become a swipe with a rule of dots beneath — the resting one filled, and no numeral.

Tapping a plate only sets a leaning: Tap one to sit with it. Nothing is sent until you hold the act. The held act then names the option she chose. A typed name is optional here; leave it empty and the choice is recorded as confirmed rather than signed.

The word that settles a choice is Chosen — never Approved. An option is not an edition.

The app · 08

Remind me, and the lock screen

Remind me holds the reminders and changes nothing about the answer. Four words, and no others. Chosen after midnight, tomorrow morning means the next 8am — hours away, not a day.

Past its date the block is not there at all, and its place says why: This one is past its date. The reminders stay until it’s answered.

On the lock screen

The notice speaks in her designer’s voice — Leah asked for your approval — and never in a warning register. It carries two acts: Open, and Ask a question, which lands in the project’s own thread rather than an inbox.

For the walk

What to try

  • Open an approval from the email link and watch where it lands — the app if it is installed, the anchor on her page if not.
  • Read the why, and check who signed it.
  • Press Approve with the name field empty. The act should stay unlit.
  • Type a full name, then tap once. Nothing should be sent.
  • Press and hold, then let go early. The fill should empty and nothing should settle.
  • Hold it through, and watch the mark settle.
  • Return an edition with a note, then find that note under The Discussion.
  • Hold one, and check the word is HELD.
  • Sign a proposal and read the seal sentence to its end.
  • Open Keep a copy, then print or save the Record of Decision.
  • Answer a choice with two plates, then one with three — tap first, then hold.
  • Set Remind me to tomorrow morning; then set the cadence under Reminders in Settings.

For the walk

What would be a defect

These are refusals, not preferences. If one of them turns up, that is the bug.

  • Anything reading red or green. Marks are mocha and the palette stays warm.
  • The words gate, task, overdue, dashboard, or AI on any screen she can reach.
  • A numeral standing where a word would do.
  • A checkmark, a badge, or a coloured pill used to carry a status.
  • A tap that submits an answer.
  • A name asked for a Return or a Hold.
  • A seal sentence naming a person where the studio should stand.
  • A receipt claiming a consequence it cannot name.
  • A mark with a fill, a shadow, or an animation that runs again on a later visit.
  • An IP address, or a full checksum, on a Record of Decision.
  • Mail before 8am, or a buzz after 8pm, in her own time zone.
  • A screen that counts her open work at her rather than naming it.

Honest edges

What is not in this build

Deferred

  • The arrival fold — the letter that arrives closed and unfolds. The flag and the measurement it depended on no longer exist, and there is no live traffic to measure against.
  • A household login — a second person in the house who can answer. Greenfield authentication; its own program, not this one.
  • The rich lock screen — the acts and the voice ship; the image attachment needs its own extension, provisioning and archive.

Never rendered

A baseline beside the cost delta. Nothing carries the figure yet, so the delta stands alone.

Still owed

A pass on real glass. Every claim on these pages rests on simulator walks and browser walks — nothing in build 4 has been seen on a device.

Beta review has not been submitted, so the external group still sits on build 3, and the widget has never been seen by anyone.
